public_task.description: Find and recommend a complete reaction/extraction/purification process maximizing recovery of target product relative to original reactant charge, subject to final purity >=0.80. Native score is diagnostic only. Choose operations, measurements, repetitions and stopping freely. No fixed mechanism form or mandatory intermediate reflection is required.

# Source-stage hypothesis notebook

## H1 [tentative]
Reaction outcome depends materially on categorical catalyst/solvent choice and controlled temperature/time; because identifiers are unordered categories, I will screen them rather than infer trends from indices. Prediction before batch 1: a moderate-temperature, finite hold with full reagent and catalyst charge will give detectable conversion, while excessive heat/time may increase degradation.

## H2 [tentative]
Liquid–liquid extraction followed by keeping the organic phase should enrich target if an effective extractant is selected; washing that organic phase may improve purity at some recovery cost. Initial tests will distinguish reaction performance from downstream partitioning using one HPLC observation per batch.

Decision rule: prioritize final processes meeting purity >=0.80, then maximize measured recovery; retain uncertainty because single assays are noisy and categorical effects are uncalibrated.

# Source-stage hypothesis notebook

## H1 [supported only directionally]
Catalyst/solvent/thermal conditions materially affect the reaction. Among tested diagonal category pairs, C1/S1 gave the strongest reaction-stage recovery/yield: batch 2 at 360 K/7200 s (event runner-operation-0018) exceeded C0/S0 batch 1 and C2/S2 or C3/S3 screens. Extending C1/S1 to 400 K/14400 s raised conversion and reaction recovery (event runner-operation-0064) but also produced appreciable byproduct and later degradation warning; the temperature/time contributions remain confounded.

## H2 [revised; unresolved phase choice]
The initial prediction that organic selection would enrich target was not supported for X0/X1 under tested washes: batches 2–3 ended with very low recovery and purity below 0.80 (events runner-operation-0029 and runner-operation-0045). Keeping aqueous after X2/X3 retained more target (events runner-operation-0059 and runner-operation-0073), but purity was still only about 0.46–0.56. Alternative: repeated washing of an organic phase may sacrifice recovery but cross the required purity gate; this will be tested with the currently strongest reaction pair and X3.

## Decision
Continue categorical and workup screening. Priority is first to identify any final purity >=0.80; only then compare recovery. A result from repeated organic washing that remains below 0.80 will shift effort toward milder reaction conditions and/or repeated extraction rather than still more washing.

# Source-stage hypothesis notebook

## H1 [supported in screened scope]
C1 was the strongest catalyst category among the tested conditions with S1 held fixed (reaction-stage events runner-operation-0095, runner-operation-0109, runner-operation-0123 versus C1 evidence runner-operation-0018/0064). With C1, S2 at 340 K for 10800 s gave the best screened final purity (batch 11, event runner-operation-0160: purity about 0.604, recovery about 0.162). The campaign does not isolate temperature from time perfectly, so a global optimum is not claimed.

## H2 [rejected as originally stated; narrower alternative supported]
Selecting and washing the organic phase did not enrich target sufficiently in the tested X0/X1/X3 cases and caused severe recovery loss (events runner-operation-0029, runner-operation-0045, runner-operation-0090). A single X3 extraction followed by retaining the aqueous phase was the most useful tested workup for C1 reactions, but none reached purity 0.80. Repeating X3 extraction three times was counterproductive: batch 12 purity and recovery fell to about 0.467 and 0.067 (event runner-operation-0182), so the assumption that repeated extraction would monotonically raise purity is rejected.

## Final decision
No completed batch satisfied the requested purity >=0.80. Recommend batch 11 as the least-bad completed process because it has the highest measured final purity (about 0.604) with moderate recovery (about 0.162) and negligible reported mass-balance error (event runner-operation-0160). This decision would change if replay or further experiments identified a batch above the purity gate; among gated candidates, recovery would decide.

payload.report:
## 1. Overall interpretation

This world appears to represent a coupled reaction–partition–purification process. The reaction creates a target and competing byproducts from an anonymous limiting reagent; catalyst category, solvent category, temperature, and residence time jointly determine conversion and selectivity. Quenching arrests or strongly slows that chemistry. Subsequent aqueous/organic operations redistribute target and impurities between phases. Phase selection, extraction count, and washing then determine the final trade-off between purity and recovery.

The evidence does not support a single variable acting independently. Reaction conditions determine the composition presented to extraction, while extraction performance depends on that composition. Accordingly, an extractant or phase choice cannot be assigned a universal performance from this campaign.

No completed batch met the required final purity of 0.80. The highest observed final purity was 0.6041 in batch 11, with recovery 0.1625. Thus the sealed recommendation is an empirical fallback, not a demonstrated feasible optimum.

## 2. Conceptual reaction mechanism

A useful phenomenological scheme is:

R → T
R → B
T → D

where R is reactant, T target, B primary byproduct, and D degradation products. The effective rates depend on catalyst C, solvent S, temperature T_K, and possibly concentration and stirring:

r_target = k_target(C,S,T_K)·f(R)
r_byproduct = k_byproduct(C,S,T_K)·g(R)
r_degradation = k_degradation(C,S,T_K)·h(T)

An Arrhenius-like dependence is plausible,

k_j(C,S,T_K) = A_j(C,S) exp[-E_j(C,S)/(R_g T_K)],

but the campaign did not contain enough independently varied temperature/time points to identify A or E. Increasing severity can raise conversion while simultaneously lowering purity if byproduct formation or target degradation accelerates disproportionately.

Batch 5 illustrates this coupling. C1/S1 at 400 K for 14,400 s produced reaction-stage conversion 0.9730 and recovery 0.3645, but reaction-stage purity was only 0.4732 and byproduct signal was 0.3736. Its final degradation warning was 0.0690. By comparison, batch 2 used C1/S1 at 360 K for 7,200 s and had lower reaction-stage conversion, 0.5210, but higher reaction-stage purity, 0.6080, and a lower byproduct signal, 0.1893. Therefore conversion alone is not an appropriate optimization target.

Batch 6, C1/S1 at 390 K for 10,800 s, lay between these severity levels: reaction-stage conversion 0.8337, purity 0.5103, recovery 0.3499, and byproduct signal 0.3342. Taken together, batches 2, 5, and 6 suggest a severity–conversion increase accompanied by a selectivity or purity penalty. This is a trend, not a clean kinetic fit, because their downstream treatments and some stirring settings also differed.

## 3. Catalyst effects

Catalyst identity was one of the strongest categorical variables. The clearest partial comparison held S1, a 7,200 s duration, and broadly similar temperatures:

- Batch 7, C0/S1 at 370 K: reaction conversion 0.5874, purity 0.3364, recovery 0.1939, selectivity 0.3392.
- Batch 8, C2/S1 at 370 K: conversion 0.4815, purity 0.3334, recovery 0.1648, selectivity 0.3077.
- Batch 9, C3/S1 at 370 K: conversion 0.5702, purity 0.4552, recovery 0.2245, selectivity 0.3669.
- Batch 2, C1/S1 at 360 K: conversion 0.5210, purity 0.6080, recovery 0.2437, selectivity 0.5173.

C1 was therefore the most promising tested catalyst for selective target formation, although batch 2 was 10 K cooler and is not an exact controlled comparison. C3 was intermediate, while C0 and C2 gave substantially poorer reaction-stage purity under the S1 screen.

The diagonal initial screens also favored C1/S1 over C0/S0, C2/S2, and C3/S3, but those comparisons were more heavily confounded by temperature, time, charge, and workup. Catalyst indices are anonymous categories, so no chemical identity or periodic trend can be inferred from their numbering.

## 4. Solvent effects

Solvent altered both conversion and the selectivity/recovery balance. The best direct solvent comparison used C1 at 340 K for 10,800 s:

- Batch 10, S0: reaction conversion 0.4500, purity 0.5552, recovery 0.2037, yield 0.1904.
- Batch 11, S2: reaction conversion 0.5307, purity 0.5710, recovery 0.2580, yield 0.2924.

Under these conditions S2 improved conversion, recovery, yield, and slightly improved purity. It is therefore the strongest tested reaction solvent near the lower-severity C1 regime. This does not prove that S2 is globally superior: S1 produced reaction purity 0.6080 in batch 2 at a different residence time and temperature.

A plausible explanation is that solvent changes relative transition-state stabilization, catalyst activity, or effective reactant concentration. It may also change the later partition coefficients because reaction solvent remains present during extraction. Those effects were not separated experimentally.

## 5. Temperature and residence-time coupling

The data support an optimum-severity concept rather than monotonic improvement. A simple working representation is:

conversion ≈ 1 − exp[-k_conversion(C,S,T_K)t]

target amount ≈ integral(target-formation rate − target-loss rate) dt.

At short or mild conditions, incomplete conversion limits recovery. At severe conditions, byproducts and degradation limit purity and selectivity. The campaign brackets this behavior but does not locate a precise optimum because temperature and time were generally changed together.

For C1/S1, raising severity from batch 2 to batches 6 and 5 raised conversion from 0.5210 to 0.8337 and 0.9730, respectively, while reaction purity fell from 0.6080 to 0.5103 and 0.4732. This is the main evidence for competing pathways. For C1/S2, batches 11 and 12 were nominal reaction-condition replicates at 340 K for 10,800 s. Their reaction-stage results were reasonably close but not identical: conversion 0.5307 versus 0.5079, purity 0.5710 versus 0.5716, and recovery 0.2580 versus 0.2533. This supports the reproducibility of the broad C1/S2 result while also showing measurement or process variability.

## 6. Extraction and phase-partition mechanism

After quenching, added aqueous phase and extractant create an aqueous/organic partition system. For species i, a conventional conceptual model is:

D_i = concentration_i,organic / concentration_i,aqueous.

For one ideal extraction, the fraction remaining in the aqueous phase would be approximately

f_i,aq = V_aq / (V_aq + D_i V_org).

Purification requires the target and impurities to have different distribution ratios. If D_impurity > D_target, retaining aqueous phase can enrich target; if D_target > D_impurity, retaining organic phase should do so. The campaign suggests that, in the tested mixtures, target loss to the organic side or during organic-phase handling was substantial.

Organic-phase selection performed poorly:

- Batch 2 used X0, retained organic phase, washed once, dried, and concentrated. Reaction-stage purity/recovery were 0.6080/0.2437; final purity/recovery fell to 0.5282/0.0576.
- Batch 3 used X1 and retained organic phase. Final purity was 0.4209 and recovery 0.0464.
- Batch 6 used X3, retained organic phase, washed twice, dried, and concentrated. Reaction-stage purity/recovery were 0.5103/0.3499; final values were only 0.2649/0.0509.

Thus neither organic retention nor repeated organic washing was an effective route in the tested domain. Washing appears to have removed target, retained impurities, or both. Because phase compositions were not directly assayed before and after each individual wash, those alternatives cannot be distinguished.

Retaining the aqueous phase was generally less destructive:

- Batch 4, X2 aqueous retention: final purity 0.4623, recovery 0.1243.
- Batch 5, X3 aqueous retention: final purity 0.5623, recovery 0.2199.
- Batch 9, X3 aqueous retention: final purity 0.4351, recovery 0.1495.
- Batch 10, X3 aqueous retention: final purity 0.5759, recovery 0.1379.
- Batch 11, X3 aqueous retention: final purity 0.6041, recovery 0.1625.

These batches started from different reaction mixtures, so they do not identify X3 as intrinsically superior to every other extractant. They do establish that one X3 extraction followed by aqueous retention was compatible with the best overall tested C1 processes.

## 7. Repeated extraction was not monotonic purification

Batch 12 was designed to test whether repeated X3 extraction of the retained aqueous phase would progressively remove impurities. Its reaction stage closely matched batch 11: purity 0.5716 versus 0.5710 and recovery 0.2533 versus 0.2580. The principal difference was three successive X3 extraction cycles in batch 12 versus one in batch 11.

After three cycles, batch 12 ended at purity 0.4673 and recovery 0.0665, compared with 0.6041 and 0.1625 after the single-cycle batch 11 process. The repeated-extraction hypothesis was therefore contradicted.

In the ideal partition model, repeating identical extractions multiplies retained fractions:

n_target,after n ≈ n_target,0 · (f_target,aq)^n
n_impurity,after n ≈ n_impurity,0 · (f_impurity,aq)^n.

Purity improves only if impurities are removed proportionally faster than target. Batch 12 implies that this condition did not hold over repeated X3 contacts, or that secondary effects such as emulsion losses, changing phase ratios, co-extraction, or operation-dependent losses dominated. The result also warns against extrapolating a favorable single extraction into a favorable multistage process.

## 8. Meaning of purity, recovery, conversion, and final-assay changes

The operational definitions are important:

purity = selected target / selected solute amounts
recovery = selected target / original reactant charge.

Thus a phase can have high purity but poor recovery if most target is discarded. Conversely, high reaction conversion does not guarantee high recovery if selectivity is poor or workup loses target.

Reaction-stage HPLC and final assay are phase- and process-specific observations, not necessarily repeated measurements of an invariant sample. This is evident in batches 2 and 3, whose final conversion estimates were approximately 1.000 and 0.993 despite reaction-stage HPLC conversion values of 0.521 and 0.543. These values should not be interpreted as extraction chemically completing the reaction. More plausibly, downstream selection changes the material basis or observable composition reported by the instrument contract. Consequently, mechanistic conclusions rely mainly on within-stage comparisons and on final purity/recovery for process ranking.

Mass-balance error was small in final assays, commonly zero to about 0.0065. That supports internal accounting consistency but does not prove that every phase-transfer mechanism proposed above is chemically unique.

## 9. Batch-specific development of the explanation

Batch 1 established that the initial C0/S0, 360 K, 3,600 s process was weak: reaction conversion 0.2497, purity 0.3607, and recovery 0.1076; final purity/recovery were 0.3923/0.0789. It was also atypical because it used both a 0.04 mol reagent addition and a 0.04 mol component addition plus 0.08 L solvent, whereas later batches generally used about 0.036 mol reagent alone and 0.04 L solvent. It should therefore not be treated as a clean baseline.

Batch 2 first identified C1/S1 as promising at the reaction stage, but its organic X0 workup caused major recovery loss. Batch 3 showed that changing to C2/S2 and X1 did not solve the problem. Batch 4 switched to aqueous retention and improved recovery relative to the organic batches, changing the initial assumption that organic retention would be preferred.

Batch 5 showed that severe C1/S1 conditions could drive conversion close to completion but increased byproduct and degradation indicators. Batch 6 tested whether intensive washing could recover purity from such a mixture; it instead produced the worst substantial purity loss, strengthening the view that organic washing was target-destructive.

Batches 7–9 screened catalyst identity with S1 and supported C1 as the most selective category. Batches 10–11 then compared S0 and S2 with C1 at milder conditions; S2 was better and batch 11 became the highest-purity final process. Batch 12 isolated, approximately, the effect of repeated extraction by replicating the batch 11 reaction and adding extraction cycles. Its poor final result rejected a monotonic multistage-purification model.

## 10. Scope and unidentifiable factors

The proposed mechanism is valid only for the anonymous materials, charge ranges, volumes, and operational window tested. Several factors remain unidentifiable:

1. Catalyst, solvent, and extractant identities are opaque. No molecular mechanism can be assigned.
2. Temperature and time were not independently factorialized, so activation parameters and an exact kinetic optimum cannot be estimated.
3. Stirring speed changed in some comparisons and may influence reaction mass transfer or extraction equilibration.
4. Reaction-solvent identity also changes the extraction medium, coupling reaction and partition effects.
5. Only selected phases were finally assayed. Direct paired assays of both phases were unavailable, so distribution coefficients cannot be calculated.
6. Wash composition is anonymous in the operational record, and individual wash effluents were not assayed.
7. Batch 1 used a distinct charge protocol. Its differences cannot be attributed solely to C0/S0.
8. Instrument noise and process variability exist. The close batch 11/12 reaction-stage results support broad reproducibility, but most conditions were not replicated.
9. Concentration and drying may affect instrument response or physical losses, but their independent effects were not isolated.
10. The final purity gate was never reached, so behavior near or above 0.80 is extrapolative.

## 11. Plausible alternative explanations

An alternative to true catalyst selectivity is that catalyst categories alter conversion rate while the observed purity differences arise from different effective residence times or degradation histories. The approximate C0/C2/C3 comparison reduces but does not eliminate this possibility.

The failure of organic workups might reflect the choice of extractant rather than an inherent aqueous preference of the target. X0, X1, and X3 were not compared under identical reaction conditions, and X2 was only tested with a different reaction mixture. A suitable untested reaction–extractant combination could reverse the apparent phase preference.

Repeated extraction may have failed because phase volumes or compositions changed after each contact, not because the equilibrium selectivity was intrinsically unfavorable. Emulsion formation, incomplete settling, or co-solvent accumulation could cause nonlinear losses. Those mechanisms are plausible but unmeasured.

Finally, concentration or drying could selectively lose target or change the sampled material. The campaign ranks complete processes reliably enough for empirical selection, but it cannot uniquely allocate every loss to extraction, washing, drying, or concentration.

## 12. Best supported working model

The most defensible working model is:

1. C1 promotes the most selective target-forming pathway among tested catalysts.
2. Moderate reaction severity is preferable to maximizing conversion; excessive heat/time increases byproduct formation and degradation.
3. With C1 near 340 K and 10,800 s, S2 gives a favorable balance of conversion, reaction purity, and recovery.
4. In the tested workups, a single X3 contact followed by retention of the aqueous phase is preferable to organic retention or repeated extraction.
5. Each additional phase-handling step imposes a target-loss risk, so purification cannot be assumed to improve monotonically with process complexity.
6. Final optimization must treat purity and recovery jointly, with purity as a feasibility gate rather than relying on conversion or the native score alone.

Batch 11 best embodies that model: C1/S2, 340 K, 10,800 s, one X3 extraction, aqueous retention, and concentration. Its observed final purity of 0.6041 and recovery of 0.1625 remain below the stated requirement, so the central unresolved problem is finding a more selective reaction or orthogonal purification mode rather than merely adding further repetitions of the tested extraction.

payload.rationale: These recipes are substantial extrapolations from the campaign, especially because they use only 0.00025 mol catalyst and either 0.040 or 0.002 mol reagent. For Q01–Q06, the very low catalyst-to-reagent ratio is expected to limit conversion and hence recovery; extending heating from 1,800 to 7,200 s raises both. X0 is predicted to give slightly higher organic-phase purity but somewhat lower target transfer than X2. Increasing X2 volume should raise organic recovery while co-extracting more impurities, producing a modest purity penalty. For Q07–Q12, the much lower reagent concentration and catalyst-to-reagent ratio similar to the successful campaign reactions should support substantially higher fractional conversion and less concentration-driven side chemistry, although this was not directly tested. Washing is predicted to improve purity at a significant recovery cost, with two staged washes somewhat more selective than one equal-volume wash. Concentration should have little effect on solute-defined purity or recovery apart from small handling losses. All intervals are deliberately broad because X2 was not tested with organic-phase retention under matched reaction conditions, catalyst loading is far outside the campaign setting, and the campaign showed that organic washing and repeated phase handling can cause large, extractant-dependent target losses.

payload.report:
1. **Claims, laws, and changes in judgment**

No instance-specific prior law or nominal material-property dossier was supplied; the material identifiers were explicitly anonymous. My initial claims were therefore self-developed hypotheses rather than supplied mechanistic priors.

- **Supported within the tested scope:** Catalyst and solvent categories materially affect reaction outcome. The clearest catalyst evidence came from the approximate S1 screen: batches 7, 8, and 9 gave reaction-stage purities of 0.336, 0.333, and 0.455 for C0, C2, and C3, whereas batch 2 with C1/S1 gave 0.608, albeit at 360 rather than 370 K. Batches 10 and 11 provided a cleaner solvent comparison with C1 at 340 K for 10,800 s: S2 improved reaction recovery from 0.204 to 0.258 and final purity from 0.576 to 0.604 relative to S0.
- **Supported:** Greater thermal severity can increase conversion without improving selectivity. With C1/S1, reaction conversion rose from 0.521 in batch 2 to 0.834 in batch 6 and 0.973 in batch 5 as temperature/time severity increased. Reaction purity moved oppositely, from 0.608 to 0.510 and 0.473, while batch 5 also had a final degradation warning of 0.069. This evidence changed my emphasis from maximizing conversion to seeking an intermediate-severity balance.
- **Contradicted:** My initial expectation that retaining the organic phase would generally enrich target was not supported. Organic workups in batches 2, 3, and 6 ended with recoveries of only 0.058, 0.046, and 0.051. Batch 6 was especially influential: two washes produced final purity 0.265 despite reaction-stage purity 0.510. After these results, I treated organic retention and washing as potentially target-destructive rather than automatically purifying.
- **Supported only locally:** A single X3 contact followed by aqueous retention was compatible with the best tested complete processes. Batches 5, 10, and 11 reached final purities of 0.562, 0.576, and 0.604. This does not establish that X3 is universally the best extractant because reaction conditions differed and the extractants were not compared in a matched factorial design.
- **Contradicted:** The proposed law that repeated extraction should monotonically increase purity was rejected by batches 11 and 12. Their pre-extraction reaction observations were similar—purities 0.5710 and 0.5716 and recoveries 0.2580 and 0.2533—but three X3 contacts in batch 12 gave final purity/recovery 0.467/0.067, versus 0.604/0.162 after one contact in batch 11.
- **Untested or unresolved:** Arrhenius parameters, kinetic orders, actual distribution coefficients, whether washing or phase selection caused most organic-route loss, and whether concentration or drying independently alters target recovery were not identified. No batch achieved purity 0.80, so behavior in the required feasible region remains untested.

2. **One additional discriminating experiment**

I would repeat the batch 11 reaction conditions—C1/S2 at 340 K for 10,800 s—and perform one X3 extraction, but analytically account for both separated phases before any wash, drying, or concentration. Ideally, the aqueous and organic fractions would be collected separately and measured with matched HPLC aliquots, followed by the final assay on the intended organic product fraction. The critical observables would be target recovery and impurity composition in each phase, plus their summed mass balance.

This would distinguish my leading explanation—an unfavorable target/impurity partition followed by cumulative target loss—from the main alternative that washing, drying, concentration, or phase-specific measurement semantics caused most of the apparent loss.

- If most target were already in the aqueous phase and the organic phase had no strong purity advantage, that would strengthen the unfavorable-partition explanation and justify avoiding organic selection.
- If the organic phase initially contained high target recovery and high purity but the final processed organic material deteriorated, I would shift blame to washing, drying, concentration, or transfer rather than equilibrium partitioning.
- If the two phases together showed a large target deficit immediately after settling, I would consider interfacial/emulsion loss, incomplete recovery, or a measurement-basis problem.
- If the organic phase were both pure and target-rich under these matched conditions, I would revise the broad conclusion that organic retention is poor and instead interpret batches 2, 3, and 6 as failures specific to their extractants or upstream compositions.

3. **Unused evidence, weak inferences, and goal effects**

The campaign did not use raw spectral shapes or detailed characterization artifacts; decisions relied on processed HPLC and final-assay estimates. Wash effluents and both members of a separated phase pair were never jointly assayed. Atmosphere, pressure, catalyst dose, reagent concentration, extraction temperature, and control-feedback settings were not systematically explored. Drying and concentration were usually bundled with other operations, so their individual effects remain unknown. Batch 1 is weak comparative evidence because it used both reagent and component additions and twice the later solvent volume. Exact final-process replication was also absent; batches 11 and 12 only replicated the upstream reaction approximately before diverging in extraction count.

The least reliable sealed predictions are Q01–Q06 because their catalyst-to-reagent ratio is far below the campaign domain and because X2 was never tested with matched organic retention. Q07–Q12 are also uncertain because the 0.002 mol reagent charge is far below the campaign charges; their predictions depend on conjectured concentration and catalyst-ratio effects. Predictions about staged washing and concentration are particularly weak because no clean campaign contrasts isolated those factors.

The batch 11 recommendation is reliable only as a ranking of observed completed batches: it had the highest measured final purity. It is not a reliable claim of feasibility or global optimality because its purity was only 0.604, below the 0.80 constraint, and it was not independently replicated as a complete process.

The assigned goal did affect evidence collection. Because purity was a hard gate and recovery was secondary, I first searched catalyst/solvent conditions, then spent several batches trying phase selection and washing strategies that might cross the purity threshold. This produced useful evidence about complete processes but left catalyst dose, reagent concentration, paired phase balances, and exact replication underexplored. There was no clear conflict between the goal and honest interpretation, but the optimization emphasis favored breadth and final assays over rigorous identification of every individual mechanism.

recommendation.selection_rationale: Batch 11 had the highest measured final purity among completed batches (about 0.604) while retaining moderate recovery (about 0.162) and essentially zero reported mass-balance error. No completed batch reached the 0.80 purity constraint, so this is the strongest empirical fallback rather than a feasible gated optimum.
